items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the thin, solid outer layer of the Earth, 5-10 km thick under oceans and up to about 70 km under continents”.
items.answer: Crust
items.markingKey: Crust: the thin, solid outer layer of the Earth, 5-10 km thick under oceans and up to about 70 km under continents. [1]

items.stem: Explain why volcanoes form at destructive plate boundaries.
items.answer: The oceanic plate is subducted into the mantle; friction and heat (and water released from the sinking plate) melt rock to form magma, which rises through cracks in the overriding plate and erupts.
items.markingKey: 1 mark subduction; 1 mark melting; 1 mark magma rises [3]

items.stem: Explain why earthquakes occur at conservative boundaries.
items.answer: The plates move past each other but friction makes them stick; stress builds up until the rocks suddenly slip, releasing energy as seismic waves.
items.markingKey: 1 mark plates stick; 1 mark stress released suddenly [2]

items.stem: Fig. 2.1 is a world map showing plate boundaries. Boundary A runs north-south down the middle of the Atlantic Ocean; arrows point away from it. Boundary B runs along the west coast of South America; an arrow on the Nazca plate points east towards the South American plate. Boundary C runs through California; arrows on each side point in opposite directions parallel to the boundary. Suggest why boundary B is more hazardous to people than boundary A.
items.answer: B has explosive volcanoes and very large earthquakes and tsunamis near cities such as Santiago and Lima; A is mostly under the ocean with gentle eruptions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark hazard size; 1 mark population exposed [2]

items.stem: Fig. 2.1 is a world map showing plate boundaries. Boundary A runs north-south down the middle of the Atlantic Ocean; arrows point away from it. Boundary B runs along the west coast of South America; an arrow on the Nazca plate points east towards the South American plate. Boundary C runs through California; arrows on each side point in opposite directions parallel to the boundary. (a) Name the type of plate boundary at A, B and C. (b) Suggest why boundary B is more hazardous to people than boundary A.
items.answer: (a) A constructive; B destructive; C conservative. (b) B has explosive volcanoes and very large earthquakes and tsunamis near cities such as Santiago and Lima; A is mostly under the ocean with gentle eruptions.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for two correct, 2 marks for three [2] (b) 1 mark hazard size; 1 mark population exposed [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 2.1, a map of plate boundaries. At A, in the Atlantic, the plates move apart. At B, off Chile and Peru, the Nazca plate moves towards the South American plate and a deep trench lies offshore. At C, the San Andreas Fault, the Pacific and North American plates move side by side. (a) Describe the landforms and hazards found at A. (b) Suggest why boundary B is more hazardous to people than boundary A.
items.answer: (a) A mid-ocean ridge with fissure eruptions of runny basaltic lava, shield volcanoes (e.g. Iceland) and small shallow earthquakes. (b) B has explosive volcanoes and very large earthquakes and tsunamis near cities such as Santiago and Lima; A is mostly under the ocean with gentle eruptions.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark landform; 1 mark hazard [2] (b) 1 mark hazard size; 1 mark population exposed [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “The mantle is a layer of liquid lava.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. The mantle is mostly solid rock that flows very slowly; only small amounts melt to form magma.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Fig. 2.1 is a world map showing plate boundaries. Boundary A runs north-south down the middle of the Atlantic Ocean; arrows point away from it. Boundary B runs along the west coast of South America; an arrow on the Nazca plate points east towards the South American plate. Boundary C runs through California; arrows on each side point in opposite directions parallel to the boundary. (a) Explain why there is a deep ocean trench at B. (b) Explain why there are no volcanoes at C. (c) Suggest why boundary B is more hazardous to people than boundary A.
items.answer: (a) The denser oceanic Nazca plate bends and is subducted beneath the continental South American plate, forming a trench. (b) Crust is neither created nor destroyed; the plates slide past each other, so no magma is produced. (c) B has explosive volcanoes and very large earthquakes and tsunamis near cities such as Santiago and Lima; A is mostly under the ocean with gentle eruptions.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark subduction; 1 mark denser oceanic plate [2] (b) 1 mark no subduction/rifting; 1 mark no magma [2] (c) 1 mark hazard size; 1 mark population exposed [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the point underground where rocks break and an earthquake starts”.
items.answer: Focus
items.markingKey: Focus: the point underground where rocks break and an earthquake starts. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between the focus and the epicentre of an earthquake.
items.answer: The focus is the point underground where rocks break and energy is released; the epicentre is the point on the surface directly above the focus.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain why shallow-focus earthquakes usually cause more damage than deep-focus ones.
items.answer: Seismic waves travel a shorter distance to the surface and lose less energy, so surface shaking is stronger.
items.markingKey: 1 mark shorter distance; 1 mark stronger shaking [2]

items.stem: Name one example of an earthquake you have studied and, for that example, describe and explain the primary and secondary effects of the earthquake.
items.answer: the Gorkha earthquake, Nepal, 2015: About 9000 deaths and 22 000 injured; over 600 000 houses and historic temples in Kathmandu destroyed; landslides blocked roads and cut off mountain villages; an avalanche on Everest killed 19 climbers; tourism income collapsed.

items.stem: Explain how an earthquake at sea can cause a tsunami.
items.answer: Sudden uplift of the sea floor at a subduction zone displaces a huge volume of water; the waves travel quickly across the ocean and grow taller as they reach shallow water near the coast.

items.stem: Explain why composite volcanoes have steep sides.
items.answer: Their lava is viscous and does not flow far before cooling, so it builds up close to the vent with layers of ash.

items.stem: Explain why shield volcanoes have gentle slopes.
items.answer: Runny, low-silica basaltic lava flows long distances before solidifying, spreading out into a wide, low dome.

items.stem: Name one example of a volcanic eruption you have studied and, for that example, explain the causes of the eruption.
items.answer: Mount Merapi, Indonesia, 2010: Merapi is a composite volcano on the destructive boundary where the Indo-Australian plate subducts beneath the Eurasian plate; melting produces viscous, gas-rich magma that builds lava domes; in October-November 2010 dome collapses produced pyroclastic flows.

items.stem: Explain why many people continue to live near active volcanoes.
items.answer: Fertile volcanic soils give high crop yields; geothermal energy and tourism provide jobs and income; minerals can be mined; families have lived there for generations; eruptions are infrequent and many can be predicted.

items.stem: Explain why many large cities have grown on or near plate boundaries.
items.answer: Coastal sites and natural harbours, flat land, routes and trade grew there long before risks were understood; examples include Tokyo, Lima and Los Angeles. Once a city exists, jobs keep people there.

items.stem: Explain how scientists can predict volcanic eruptions.
items.answer: Rising magma causes small earthquakes (seismometers), swelling of the ground (tiltmeters, GPS, satellites), increased gas emissions and higher ground temperatures; these signs can give days or weeks of warning.

items.stem: Explain how building design can reduce deaths in an earthquake.
items.answer: Cross-bracing and steel frames let buildings sway without collapsing; base isolators absorb shaking; lightweight roofs reduce weight; automatic shutters stop glass falling.

items.answer: Nepal (Gorkha earthquake, 2015): Before: a building code existed but was poorly enforced; some schools had drills. After: international rescue teams, Indian and Chinese army helicopters, tents and water from NGOs; reconstruction grants to rebuild houses with earthquake-resistant designs.

items.stem: Describe the differences between oceanic and continental crust.
items.answer: Oceanic: thinner (5-10 km), denser (basalt), younger, can be subducted. Continental: thicker (up to 70 km), less dense (granite), older, not subducted.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each valid comparison up to [3]

items.stem: At the San Andreas Fault in California, the Pacific and North American plates move past each other at about 4 cm per year. Calculate how far the plates move in 5 000 000 years. Give your answer in km.
items.answer: 200 km

items.stem: “Destructive plate boundaries are more hazardous to people than constructive plate boundaries.” Discuss this view, using named examples, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: earthquake magnitude; types of eruption.
items.answer: For: They produce the largest earthquakes (Tōhoku 2011, magnitude 9.0), tsunamis and explosive eruptions (Merapi 2010). Many densely populated cities lie near them, e.g. Tokyo, Jakarta, Lima. Against: Constructive boundaries can be hazardous: Eyjafjallajökull (2010) disrupted about 100 000 flights; Laki (1783) caused famine. Conservative boundaries also cause deadly earthquakes (Haiti 2010). Risk depends on vulnerability and preparation as much as boundary type. Judgement: Generally true because of the scale of hazards at subduction zones, but the impact depends on population and level of development.

items.stem: Explain why the number of deaths from an earthquake does not depend only on its magnitude.
items.answer: It also depends on depth, distance to cities, population density, building quality, time of day, preparedness and speed of rescue; e.g. Haiti 2010 (7.0) killed far more than Tōhoku 2011 (9.0) killed in collapsing buildings.

items.stem: Earthquake P had a magnitude of 4.5 and earthquake Q a magnitude of 7.5. Each increase of 1 on the magnitude scale means about 10 times more ground movement and about 32 times more energy released. Calculate how many times more energy earthquake Q released.
items.answer: about 32 768 times

items.stem: “Secondary effects of earthquakes are more serious than primary effects.” Discuss this view, using named examples, and reach a supported conclusion.
items.answer: For: Tōhoku (2011): the tsunami caused over 90% of deaths and the Fukushima nuclear accident. Haiti (2010): cholera killed thousands in the months after. Against: In Nepal (2015) and Haiti most deaths came from buildings collapsing during the shaking. Primary effects destroy the infrastructure needed for recovery. Judgement: It depends on the event: for coastal subduction earthquakes secondary effects are often worse; for inland earthquakes primary effects usually dominate.

A steep-sided cone made of alternate layers of ash and viscous lava, with explosive eruptions.
Molten rock that has erupted onto the Earth’s surface.
A broad volcano with gentle slopes built from layers of runny basaltic lava.

items.stem: Explain how pyroclastic flows form and why they are so dangerous.
items.answer: An eruption column collapses or a lava dome breaks up, sending hot gas, ash and rock down the slope at over 100 km/h and several hundred °C; there is no time to escape and they burn and bury everything.

items.stem: Grace argues that the level of development of a country is the most important factor in reducing the impact of tectonic hazards. How far do you agree? Give evidence for and against before reaching a judgement. You may wish to consider: warning systems; Haiti and Japan; building codes.
items.answer: For: HICs such as Japan can afford building codes, warning systems and fast rescue; deaths in Christchurch (2011) were 185 compared with over 100 000 in Haiti (2010). Against: The size and type of hazard matter: Tōhoku’s tsunami killed about 18 000 people even in a well-prepared HIC. Community preparation, education and good governance can be cheap and effective in LICs (e.g. Merapi evacuation). Judgement: Development is very important because it pays for preparation and response, but hazard magnitude, location and governance also matter.

items.stem: Study Fig. 2.1, a map of plate boundaries. At A, in the Atlantic, the plates move apart. At B, off Chile and Peru, the Nazca plate moves towards the South American plate and a deep trench lies offshore. At C, the San Andreas Fault, the Pacific and North American plates move side by side. Describe the landforms and hazards found at A.
items.answer: A mid-ocean ridge with fissure eruptions of runny basaltic lava, shield volcanoes (e.g. Iceland) and small shallow earthquakes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark landform; 1 mark hazard [2]

items.stem: “Destructive plate boundaries are more hazardous to people than constructive plate boundaries.” To what extent do you agree with this statement? Support your answer with examples. You may wish to consider: population density; types of eruption.
items.answer: For: They produce the largest earthquakes (Tōhoku 2011, magnitude 9.0), tsunamis and explosive eruptions (Merapi 2010). Many densely populated cities lie near them, e.g. Tokyo, Jakarta, Lima. Against: Constructive boundaries can be hazardous: Eyjafjallajökull (2010) disrupted about 100 000 flights; Laki (1783) caused famine. Conservative boundaries also cause deadly earthquakes (Haiti 2010). Risk depends on vulnerability and preparation as much as boundary type. Judgement: Generally true because of the scale of hazards at subduction zones, but the impact depends on population and level of development.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “waves of energy released by an earthquake that travel outwards from the focus”.
items.answer: Seismic waves
items.markingKey: Seismic waves: waves of energy released by an earthquake that travel outwards from the focus. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between magnitude and intensity.
items.answer: Magnitude measures the energy released at the source (one value per earthquake); intensity (Mercalli) measures the effects at a place and decreases away from the epicentre.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Table 2.1 gives data for three earthquakes. The Gorkha earthquake, Nepal, 2015: magnitude 7.8, focus depth 15 km, deaths about 9 000, LIC. The Tōhoku earthquake, Japan, 2011: magnitude 9.0, focus depth 30 km, deaths about 18 000, HIC. The Christchurch earthquake, New Zealand, 2011: magnitude 6.2, focus depth 5 km, deaths about 185, HIC. Calculate how many times more deaths there were in the deadliest earthquake than in the least deadly.
items.answer: 97.3 times

items.stem: Table 2.1 gives data for three earthquakes. The Christchurch earthquake, New Zealand, 2011: magnitude 6.2, focus depth 5 km, deaths about 185, HIC. The Gorkha earthquake, Nepal, 2015: magnitude 7.8, focus depth 15 km, deaths about 9 000, LIC. The Haiti earthquake, 2010: magnitude 7.0, focus depth 13 km, deaths about 220 000, LIC. (a) Calculate how many times more deaths there were in the deadliest earthquake than in the least deadly. (b) Using the table, suggest whether there is a clear link between magnitude and number of deaths. (c) Explain why earthquakes in LICs often cause more deaths than those in HICs.
items.answer: (a) 1189.2 times (b) No clear link: the highest-magnitude earthquake was not the deadliest; deaths also depend on level of development, building quality, depth and population. (c) Poorly constructed buildings, little enforcement of building codes, dense informal settlements, weak emergency services and limited money for preparation and rescue.
items.markingKey: (a) 220000 ÷ 185 = 1189.2 [2] (b) 1 mark judgement; 1 mark use of data [2] (c) 1 mark each point up to [3]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “lava”?
options: The bowl-shaped hollow at the top of a volcano around the vent.
A steep-sided cone made of alternate layers of ash and viscous lava, with explosive eruptions.
A broad volcano with gentle slopes built from layers of runny basaltic lava.
Molten rock that has erupted onto the Earth’s surface.
items.answer: Molten rock that has erupted onto the Earth’s surface.
items.markingKey: Lava: molten rock that has erupted onto the Earth’s surface. [1]

items.stem: Explain how lahars can affect places many kilometres from a volcano.
items.answer: Ash mixes with rain or meltwater from snow and glaciers; the mudflow follows river valleys at high speed, burying towns and bridges far downstream (e.g. Armero, Colombia, 1985).
items.markingKey: 1 mark formation; 1 mark travel along valleys [2]

items.stem: Fig. 2.2 is a cross-section of Mount Pinatubo, Philippines, a composite volcano at a destructive boundary where the Eurasian (Philippine Sea region) plate subducts. It shows a central vent, a crater, alternate layers of ash and lava, and a secondary vent on the flank. A town of 60 000 people lies 15 km from the summit, and the authorities have set an exclusion zone of 15 km. Describe two hazards the town could face in an eruption.
items.answer: Ash fall collapsing roofs and damaging crops and lungs; pyroclastic flows; lahars along river valleys; volcanic bombs; gases.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each hazard with brief description [2]

items.stem: Name an example of a volcanic eruption. For your chosen example, describe how people responded to the eruption.
items.answer: Model answer (Eyjafjallajökull, Iceland, 2010): Rapid evacuation using warnings; roads breached to let floodwater pass; airspace closures; later new rules on safe ash levels for aircraft.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Monitoring, warnings, evacuation, shelters, aid, longer-term planning. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Volcanic soils are often very fertile.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Weathered ash and lava release minerals such as potassium and phosphorus.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Study Fig. 2.3, a description of a volcano and its surroundings. The lower slopes are densely settled with rice terraces (about 900 people per km²); the middle slopes grow coffee and vegetables and have a geothermal power station; the upper slopes are forest used by trekkers visiting the 2900 m crater. Suggest two reasons why the population density is highest below 600 m.
items.answer: Fertile volcanic soils and flatter land for rice; water from rivers; warmer; easier access and roads.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Table 2.2 shows the number of people living at different distances from Etna: 0-10 km: 160 000, 10-20 km: 170 000, 20-30 km: 190 000, 30-50 km: 260 000. (a) Calculate the total number of people living within 50 km. (b) Suggest why many people still live within 10 km of the summit.
items.answer: (a) 780 000 (b) Fertile soils, tourism and jobs, family land, and confidence in monitoring and warnings.
items.markingKey: (a) 160 + 170 + 190 + 260 = 780 thousand [1] (b) 1 mark each up to [2]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Earthquake early-warning systems can give seconds of warning.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. They detect the fast P-waves and send alerts before the more damaging S-waves arrive, giving time to stop trains and take cover.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Classify each action as prediction, preparation or emergency response, and explain one of your choices. A: Using satellites to detect swelling of a volcano. B: Installing seismometers and tiltmeters on a volcano. C: Setting up field hospitals and distributing clean water. D: Measuring sulphur dioxide emissions from the crater.
items.answer: A prediction; B prediction; C emergency response; D prediction. E.g. prediction gives warning that an event is coming; preparation reduces its impact in advance; response happens after it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for every two correct classifications; 1 mark explanation [3]

items.stem: Table 2.3 compares two earthquakes. The Christchurch earthquake, New Zealand, 2011: magnitude 6.2, HIC, about 185 deaths, about 3 million people in the affected region. The Tōhoku earthquake, Japan, 2011: magnitude 9.0, HIC, about 18 000 deaths, about 2 million people in the affected region. Calculate the number of deaths per million people in the affected region for each earthquake.
items.answer: The Christchurch earthquake, New Zealand, 2011: 62; The Tōhoku earthquake, Japan, 2011: 9000 per million

items.stem: Table 2.3 compares two earthquakes. The Tōhoku earthquake, Japan, 2011: magnitude 9.0, HIC, about 18 000 deaths, about 8 million people in the affected region. The Christchurch earthquake, New Zealand, 2011: magnitude 6.2, HIC, about 185 deaths, about 9 million people in the affected region. (a) Suggest why deaths per million people is a fairer comparison than total deaths. (b) Describe two ways in which the impacts of future earthquakes could be reduced in the poorer of these areas.
items.answer: (a) It allows for the different number of people exposed to the hazard. (b) Retrofitting schools and hospitals with cross-bracing; enforcing building codes; community drills and education; emergency supplies stored locally; hazard maps limiting building on unstable slopes.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark each developed method [2]

items.stem: For a named example of a country’s response to a tectonic hazard that you have studied, evaluate how successful the strategies were in reducing the impacts of the hazard.
items.answer: Model answer (Indonesia (Merapi eruption, 2010)): Monitoring and evacuation saved thousands of lives, but about 350 people died, some refusing to leave their farms and livestock.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: What worked and what did not, with evidence (deaths, damage, speed of response) and a judgement. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]
